presenceLabel: Mingo town, camp or raid site in this area
presenceNote: The Mingo story is shown as 1770–1776, the dated sources for Kentucky (Washington at Mingo Town 1770; Yellow Creek 1774; the Georgetown raid Dec 1776). The nation is shown c.1750–1832 (low–medium confidence): the Cayuga and Seneca lakes in New York as the origin country, Mingo Town (1770), Pluggy’s Town in Delaware County, Ohio (from 1772, county level only) and the Sandusky and Lewistown Seneca to the 1832 removal. No source locates a Mingo camp in Kentucky, so none is drawn. “Mingo” is an outsiders’ name.
overlapNote: Mingo were the Six Nations’ resident presence in Ohio and were named as parties ("Mingoes of Ohio") in the Fort Stanwix deed and attended the treaty, so this page relates directly to six-nations.json. The same small hunting camps were used by Shawnee, Delaware, Cherokee and Tutelo in the mid-1700s (Henderson 1992). Kentucky was also claimed by the Shawnee and Cherokee.
basis: Henderson 1992 (general statement), Washington’s 1770 diary (Mingo Town), Wikipedia for the Yellow Creek massacre and Pluggy, NPS/USFS for the 1776 raids. No Mingo area is drawn. Native Land Digital data was not used.

eras.label: c.1750–1769 · Cayuga and Seneca lakes, New York
eras.text: Most Mingo were Seneca and Cayuga, with some Susquehannock, who moved from New York into the Ohio Country from the mid-18th century (Wikipedia). The Cayuga lived at Cayuga Lake and the Seneca at Seneca Lake and the Genesee (Wikipedia, Haudenosaunee). The tint is an approximate general area of that origin country, built from whole counties (Cayuga, Seneca and Livingston, New York). ‘Mingo’ is an outsiders’ name, and some scholars treat it as a slur. Henderson (1992) says small Mingo, Shawnee and other hunting camps existed south of the Ohio in the mid-1700s; no source gives where any Kentucky camp was, so none is drawn.

eras.label: 1770–1771 · Mingo Town, Ohio
eras.text: Mingo of Ohio attended the 1768 Fort Stanwix treaty, which ceded the land south of the Ohio to the Crown. In Oct 1770 Washington found about 20 cabins and 70 people at Mingo Town on the Ohio (Jefferson Co., Ohio; point approximate). The tint is an approximate general area of Mingo presence on the upper Ohio, built from whole counties. Henderson (1992) says small Mingo, Shawnee and other hunting camps existed south of the river in the mid-1700s and later moved north; no source gives where any Kentucky camp was, so none is drawn.

eras.label: 1772–1773 · Pluggy’s Town, Delaware County, Ohio
eras.text: From 1772 the Mingo leader Pluggy had a town in Delaware County, Ohio, about 18 miles north of Columbus (Wikipedia, Pluggy). No source gives the town’s coordinates, so the whole county is tinted and no point is drawn. The upper Ohio tint (Mingo Town, Jefferson County) is the earlier area.

eras.label: 1774–1775 · Yellow Creek and Dunmore’s War
eras.text: Logan lived at Yellow Creek on the upper Ohio, where Virginians killed his relatives on 30 Apr 1774, leading into Dunmore’s War. The point is approximate (near the site, on the West Virginia bank), inside the tinted general area of Mingo presence on the upper Ohio. Henderson says hunting parties became raiding parties in the 1770s.

eras.label: 1776 · Raid on McClelland’s Station (Kentucky)
eras.text: On 25 Dec 1776 the Mingo chief Pluggy attacked Harrod’s Town, and on 29 Dec he attacked McClelland’s Station at Georgetown and was killed. The raiders came from the Ohio country (the tinted area: the upper Ohio and Delaware County, where Pluggy’s Town stood, location approximate). The Georgetown point marks a RAID, not a camp, and is approximate.

eras.label: c.1777–1832 · Sandusky and Lewistown Seneca
eras.text: The Seneca of Sandusky (Sandusky and Seneca counties) and the Seneca-Shawnee of Lewistown (Logan County) appear in the 1817 Treaty of Fort Meigs, which set aside 30,000 acres for the Seneca (Wyandotte archive transcription). Wikipedia says the Mingo of western Ohio sold their lands and went west to Kansas in 1832, and that the British had granted a reservation on the Sandusky River after the French and Indian War. The tint is an approximate general area built from whole counties, not a boundary. No Kentucky camp is known or drawn.

properties.label: Mingo Town (1770)
properties.name: Mingo Town, Jefferson Co. OH (1770, approximate)
properties.note: Mingo Town (Shenanjee), west bank of the Ohio a little above the Cross Creeks, Jefferson Co., Ohio: about 20 cabins and 70 Six Nations inhabitants on 22 Oct 1770 (Washington). Point is the modern Mingo Junction village (40.321, -80.609), which the editors of Washington’s papers place near the old town (Cross Creeks about 3¼ miles below Steubenville). Approximate to a few miles.

properties.label: Yellow Creek (1774)
properties.name: Yellow Creek mouth / massacre area, 1774 (approximate)
properties.note: Yellow Creek massacre, 30 Apr 1774: on the West Virginia bank across from the mouth of Yellow Creek; Logan lived at the creek mouth (Ohio side). Point is the Mountaineer Casino location given by Wikipedia as near the site. Approximate to a few miles.

properties.label: McClelland’s Station RAID, 29 Dec 1776 (a raid, not a camp)
properties.name: McClelland’s Station raid, Georgetown KY, 29 Dec 1776 (approximate)
properties.note: McClelland’s Station, Georgetown, Scott Co.: Pluggy’s Mingo raid of 29 Dec 1776 (Pluggy killed). A raid, not a camp. Point is the Georgetown town centre from Wikipedia; the station site itself is not located to better than the town.

Cayuga Lake and Seneca Lake country, New York (Cayuga, Seneca and Livingston counties), read mechanically from the lakes and the Genesee named in Wikipedia’s Haudenosaunee article. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Upper Ohio valley around Mingo Town and Yellow Creek plus Delaware County, Ohio, where Pluggy’s Town stood (about 18 miles north of Columbus; its coordinates are not sourced, so the whole county is tinted). Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

The Sandusky Seneca (Sandusky and Seneca counties) and the Lewistown Seneca-Shawnee reserve (Logan County), Ohio, named in the 1817 Treaty of Fort Meigs; whole counties. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.
